data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In engineering, safety margins often rely on statistical probability of load distribution (inductive), whereas Popperian preference explicitly rejects probability.","A chess player may prefer an opening because they believe it leads to a winning position (teleological/inductive), while the Popperian chooses a theory only because it allows for the quickest checkmate of the theory itself if it is wrong."],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that acting on a theory inherently entails a psychological or logical commitment to its future reliability, the non-inductive defense fails.","If 'severity' cannot be quantified or compared between competing theories without invoking probabilistic assumptions about test outcomes."],"shared_structure":["Selection of a strategy/tool based on past resistance to failure rather than predicted future success.","Acknowledgment that past performance does not guarantee future results but indicates robustness under stress.","Preference driven by the desire to maximize the visibility of potential errors."],"source_memory_refs":["bridge_engineering_safety_margins","chess_opening_preparation"],"transfer_claims":["Just as an engineer uses the bridge design that has withstood the strongest simulated storms not because it won't collapse next time, but because it has proven most responsive to stress analysis, the scientist chooses the corroborated theory to maximize error detection.","Preferring the most tested chess opening is rational not because it guarantees a win, but because its nuances are best understood, allowing for faster adaptation when the opponent deviates."]},"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference of future truth, but as a critical rational choice to subject one's actions to the most severe available test; accepting this costs the scientist any expectation that the chosen theory is likely true or will remain unfalsified.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent prefers the theory because they believe it is more likely to succeed in the future, the preference becomes inductive and indefensible on Popperian terms.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If no unrefuted theories exist to choose between, the mechanism defaults to selecting the theory with the highest remaining verisimilitude potential based on logical content alone.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' of accepting the theory includes an implicit bet on its continuity, the defense collapses into the pragmatism Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Preference via Severity Maximization: The agent selects the theory with the highest empirical content and best survival record solely because it offers the greatest opportunity for future error detection (falsification), thereby minimizing the risk of acting on an easily refutable dogma. This treats corroboration as a report of past test severity, not a predictor of future success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
